title: test-0031-SOC-HIS-EARLYHUMANS
passage: Rohan and his grandfather sat near the banks of the Bolan River in present-day Pakistan, looking at the ancient site of Mehrgarh. Grandfather explained that 8,000 years ago, people here stopped wandering and started farming. They didn't just catch animals; they carefully selected and bred them over generations to be gentle, which is what we call domestication. Unlike the nomadic groups who moved seasonally to follow food, these settlers built permanent mud-brick houses. They used microliths, which were tiny, sharp stone blades fixed onto wooden handles to make efficient tools for harvesting grain. These were far more advanced than the random, unshaped rocks used by earlier ancestors. Grandfather pointed to a nearby cave wall where ancient paintings showed hunters. He explained that these weren't just doodles by children, but important records of their lives. When people died, they were buried with goods like stone tools or animal remains, not because they were throwing away trash, but because they believed these items were needed in the afterlife. This transition to farming and settled life changed human history forever, allowing communities to grow and thrive in one place.
